I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum. One of my friends calls hers a marriage saver, while the other was both thrilled and horrified by how many stains the vacuum’s AI found on her floors. Personally, my robot vacuums keep me from wanting to set the litter box on fire, since my cat is on a mission to create his own navigational trail of litter through my home.

The best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to. These gadgets are mopping, scrubbing away stains, lifting themselves off obstacles, and even reminding you to clean the dirtier areas in your home more frequently. A good robot vacuum can cost a pretty penny, but it doesn’t have to, depending on what you’re looking for. Which is the best model for you? I’ve been testing every fresh robot vacuum I can in my three-story home filled with three adults, a preschooler, and a cat.

In a recent development, here are the best robot vacuum cleaners I’ve tried this year, and everything we really liked from recent years. Looking for more vacuum ideas? Don't miss our guides to the Best Dyson Vacuums, Best Cordless Vacuums, Best Vacuums for Pet Hair, Best Carpet Cleaners, and Best Vacuums.

According to recent reports, updated November 2026: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is now this guide's budget pick, with the Eufy Omni C28 as a budget runner-up. I've also added the Roborock Saros 20 Flow to Honorable Mentions, and testing notes on the Dyson Nurovi R3, Tapo RV50 Pro Omni, and three iRobot Roomba models (Max 875, Plus 678, and Plus 575). I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

I’ve been testing the latest models from our favorite cleaning brands. Here are the top three I’d buy right now.

Sources indicate that I was surprised how much I liked the AI-powered Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. Its UV light revealed spots on my floor where I know I previously had spills, and its built-in AI had the vacuum go back over to deep-clean those spots in a way I clearly hadn’t done before. The UV Reveal also did a great job on my hard floors (both LVP and tile) as a mop-and-vacuum combo, as well as on my builder-grade carpet and a large rug in the living room. I was impressed that the rug actually felt just as fluffy and well-vacuumed as if I had cracked out my favorite Dyson stick vacuum instead of just sending a robot vacuum to do the work for me.

Recent findings suggest that it has an extendable arm, which did a good job passing my corner test. I stuck three Cheerios in tricky corners of my home, and it got two out of three, doing better than the latest Dyson vacuum. It managed to get the trickier two corners too; it skipped the third Cheerio to avoid bumping my bar stools. I also did a spill test with two spots of cherry juice in my home. It mopped away the first spill with no problem, but I did have to send it back out to finish cleaning the second spill. The UV Reveal did great with obstacle avoidance and has “NeverStuck Technology” to lift itself off obstacles, and it worked to get itself off the flat, long legs of one of my side tables. The vacuum finished a cleaning run in a good amount of time, cleaning my entire main floor in about 60 minutes, but it does go back out to scrub all the spots it sees on the floor. That took another 30 minutes for me, but I assume that would get shorter over time, the longer you live with this vacuum and have it cleaning up. Still, 93 minutes to run through four rooms and go back to do some scrub work is a solid time window.

In a recent development, overall, this vacuum really shines on hard floors, but I also liked it on rugs and carpet if you have a mix of these in your home. It has an auto-empty base with a bagless debris system, so you won’t need to worry about purchasing debris bags to empty the docking station. The only downside is that the vacuum can learn only a single map, so it doesn’t work for multiple floors of your home unless you’re game for it to remap every time (which takes only a couple minutes, so it’s not a horrible experience, but the vacuum will also want the base station lugged up or down the stairs too). The suction is also a mystery; Shark has declined to comment on the exact suction. Still, we’ve loved low-suction vacuums before, and the results have been great.

Industry observers note that this vacuum is one I refuse to part with, and while its retail price is technically $800, it's on sale enough in the $500 range that this has become the budget pick I'd easily recommend when it's on sale. The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is the newest update to Roborock's more affordable Qrevo line, which went without updates for years. The Qrevo 2 Pro is cheaper than the Curv 2 that debuted in January 2026, and it still packs a ton of power, great navigation, and the same handy app. It comes with 20,000 Pa of suction, a FlexiArm mop that does a better job of corner cleaning, and a reversible side brush to help dislodge corner debris. I love seeing the arm reach out and get all the edges and corners around my house, especially underneath cabinets in the kitchen and bathroom.

The Qrevo 2 Pro also pulled ahead in some areas when compared against the similarly often-on-sale Eufy Omni C28. While the Eufy got itself stuck on cords in my bedroom, the Qrevo 2 Pro only attempted to eat cords without actually getting stuck on them. The Qrevo still isn't great at seeing small objects; it took my cat's toys for rides around the room, but they usually didn't get stuck or stop the vacuum. Both vacuums scored a 2 out of 3 on my Cheerio test, but the Qrevo 2 Pro got the harder fridge Cheerio with its FlexiArm mop. The Eufy did a little better on mopping, but neither vacuum did perfectly. I'm giving the Qrevo 2 Pro a 1.25 out of 2—one spill was just about gone, but the area around it was all slightly sticky, while the second spill was only half cleaned. It's hard to grade perfectly. It also occasionally leaves a little debris behind when it goes over thresholds that separate carpet from hard flooring, but it didn't have this glitch when transitioning onto rugs.

Recent findings suggest that this vacuum (and its base station) also looks good and is fairly quiet. (Except when it cleans on tile, which is a noisy experience as it travels across the grout divots. But it does a good job.) Both the base station and vacuum itself are quieter than the Eufy Omni C28, and it is especially pleasant if you let the Qrevo 2 Pro vacuum and mop separately. It takes longer than doing the combo cleans, but this vacuum pulled off doing both a separate vacuuming session and mopping of my massive first floor in two hours, which most vacuums still take for combo cleans.

We've loved the app and navigation from Roborock for years, and it still stands out among its rivals in this area. The Roborock only struggles to navigate on a C-shaped table with long, thin, flat legs it can't see against my wood floors. Besides that it does a fantastic job navigating around all kinds of furniture and never runs into anything the way I've seen more expensive vacuums do. It can map multiple floors of my house too. Ultimately, it's a great, well-rounded vacuum for the price.

In a recent development, if the Roborock Qrevo isn't on sale, this Eufy is the next best thing. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So previously recommended Eufy’s older X10 Pro Omni as a great robot vacuum without spending too much, and Eufy released the Eufy Omni C28 in February this year with a similar set of features and price point. The Omni C28 comes with nearly double the suction power of the older model, a self-cleaning roller mop instead of mop pads, and retractable detangling brushes.

It does a solid job mopping and vacuuming, but it has a shorter battery life, leaving it at only 37 percent after completing the four-room main floor of my house. This is a bit of a bummer, since this affordable vacuum can do multi-floor mapping. While it can store enough maps to clean all three levels of my home, it doesn’t have the battery life to do so. But it does charge fairly rapidly, and I was able to still clean all three floors of my house in a single day—I just had to let it recharge a little at the base first. It went back up to 57 percent battery life after just 20 minutes in its docking station. It also tried to eat the cords near my bed, and luckily I was nearby to yank them free. If you get this vacuum, make sure your cords are clear of the vacuum's reach.

According to recent reports, with my corner Cheerio test, this vacuum also got two out of three Cheerios, but it missed the trickier fridge-corner Cheerio. This is the hardest spot to get into, so I’m not surprised, but it does mean you’ll have to check those corners more with this vacuum. The cherry juice spill test also showed similar results: The first spot it reached was cleaned completely, while the second spot, which had more time to dry, still had some sticky residue left behind.

Overall, though, it’s a good vacuum for the price, especially since it packs multi-floor mapping, the capability to mop and vacuum, and good results all around for a vacuum that’s already usually on sale for around or under $500.

There are a lot of great robot vacuums out there. Here are a few others we’ve tried and liked.

It has been revealed that dreame L60 Ultra for $1,000: This vacuum did a good all-around job and packs a ton of good features, including dual flex arms, the EasyLeap System that lets it move over almost-2-inch tall obstacles, and 35,000 Pa of suction. This is a great one to buy if you have tall thresholds in your home thanks to that lifting feature, but otherwise, you could get a smarter vacuum for a cheaper price. This vacuum does promise dirt detection, but I never noticed it delivering on that promise. Still, my Dreame long-term tester commented that it's leagues quieter than her older Dreame vacuum, so it's a good upgrade choice if you like Dreame and want something quieter.

According to recent reports, dreame X50 Ultra for $800: If you have pets that tend to make one area of your home particularly hair- or debris-covered, this is the vacuum to get. The Dreame X50 Ultra has tons of great features, including double-roll brushes, side wands for edge cleaning, and a large-capacity docking station, but the real standout is the AI that can notice extremely dirty areas. It’s the most effective dirt- and obstacle-identification system that former WIRED editor Adrienne So has tried, and it will even remind her which areas it needs to clean more often (for her, that’s near her dog’s bed).

According to recent reports, dyson Spot+Scrub Ai for $800: The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai is a good robot vacuum overall, with a unique base station design that calls back to the Dyson stick vacuums and built-in AI to find spots and stains on your floor to scrub them away. It mostly worked, but I did prefer this feature in the Shark above, which has a similar starting retail price but is usually on sale. It’s also a little tall, so if you have builder-grade cabinets like I do, it might not be able to vacuum the toe kicks or underneath your Ikea furniture. (It got stuck underneath my Tolstad bed frame and was too tall to get underneath my Besta cabinet.).

Matic Robot Vacuum Bundle for $1,495: According to former WIRED editor Adrienne So, this vacuum is spectacular. It’s the only 10/10 rating she’s ever given a robot vacuum. Its six RGB infrared cameras do a great job making a 3D map, the single waste bag contains wet and dry debris, it does a great job cleaning toe kicks, and it was quiet enough to run without bothering So’s kids while they watched TV. That’s due to Matic’s lower suction power (only 3,200 Pa), but she didn’t notice any decrease in cleanliness as a result. It’s compact and square, giving it the ability to really get into corners. The only bummer is that it has expensive, proprietary waste bags. But those waste bags do have diaper salts, charcoal, and a HEPA filter, so you don’t have to replace the filters separately.

Narwal Flow for $849: WIRED’s Reviews team hasn’t always had success with Narwal’s vacuums, but when I tested this model late last year, I found it super easy to set up and get cleaning. I had no connectivity issues, installation was a breeze, and the app was easy to navigate. It did a good job cleaning my hard floors and rug, and even when I ran it right out of the box until it ran out of battery, it returned itself to its station to recharge and then resumed the task a few hours later, all on its own. The base station is also sleek and cute compared with the dark, bulky structures most have.

Roborock Saros 20 Flow for $1,300: If you're looking for something with serious suction, the Saros 20 Flow is my preferred choice out of Roborock's higher-power Saros line. I really like using it, and the roller mop does a good job mopping, but it only got one out of three Cheerios on my corner test and didn't manage to spot any stains on my floor, even with the promised built-in stain detection. It's the option I'd choose if you want a robot vacuum with great navigation and super-high suction (36,000 Pa) that won't deposit debris around the house like the Saros 20 tended to, but I think you'd be just as happy with a cheaper Roborock.

It has been revealed that roborock Qrevo Curv 2 for $1,000: This is another great option from Roborock and another part of the Qrevo line we've liked for years. The Qrevo Curv 2 came out in January and has similar strengths to the Qrevo 2 Pro above, but it has a roller mop called SpiraFlow instead of two individual mop pads. It also has similar struggles, with threshold debris and small objects being hard to spot. It's a good vacuum overall, and best on sale (which it often is!), but I'd pick my picks on sale over it.

Sources indicate that A robot vacuum is an automated vacuum, usually shaped like a round disc, that moves around your house to vacuum (and mop, as many models these days include mopping) on your behalf. You might’ve heard some refer to these devices as “Roombas,” which is the brand that made the concept popular, but today just about every cleaning brand—from high-end Dyson to affordable Bissell—makes some kind of robot vacuum. They come with either a charging station or a larger docking station that can self-empty.

There are a few things most robot vacuums will need to work properly:.

The Federal Communications Commission declared in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States—including robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available new models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more could be affected. For now, you'll still see vacuums launching from these brands, though, since FCC approval is given months ahead of product releases.

This decision comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which has deemed automated robotic devices a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:.

Overall, robot vacuums themselves aren’t banned, but new models from companies based outside the US won’t get FCC approval and can’t be sold in the US. You don’t need to stop using any robot vacuum you have, but if you’re in the market for a new one, it’s better to shop sooner before availability starts to decline—and prices are likely to rise as supply falls.

Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200: Dyson's newest version of the Spot+Scrub has a UV light to help its AI spot stains, and I was happy to see those stains reported in the app, but I couldn't tell if the vacuum actually did more detailed cleaning in those areas. That aside, I wanted to love this vacuum more than I did. My problem with the vacuum is how it did in regular cleaning sessions: It left pieces of popcorn behind when vacuuming on my downstairs rugs, didn't seem to ever get close enough to my walls for any kind of edge cleaning, and was too tall to get underneath cabinets or basic Ikea furniture around my house (but still smacked into that furniture over and over again due to camera placement). It also got a zero on my corner Cheerio test, failing to even get the Cheerio that just sits near a chair leg. I haven't tested either of the cheaper upcoming Dyson robot vacuum options, but if this is how the best one does, I'm not inclined to.

Eufy S2 for $950: This robot vacuum has an intense-looking base station. However, I was disappointed it missed both the fridge and bookshelf Cheerios in my corner test, giving it only a one out of three. Both cherry stains were scrubbed away, but the floor near where the stains were felt sticky all over even with the stains ostensibly wiped away. It’s especially a bummer given the price point; it needed to do better to be worth such a high price tag.

Sources indicate that iRobot Roomba Max 705 Combo for $800: The name Roomba is synonymous with robot vacuums for many people, but it’s actually a specific line made by iRobot. I really liked both the high-end look of the Max 705 Combo (not to be confused with the cheaper Max 705) and the overall job it did mopping and cleaning my floors. The app is great since it highlights you a map of where the robot went, and it’ll also show you a little itinerary of which rooms it’s doing in what order. However, setup and any resetting you need to do is a long process, so be ready to commit and troubleshoot when you unbox it. My long-term tester has also reported that its mopping abilities have not improved over the six months it's been running in her house, but it does best with vacuuming and carpet.

Recent findings suggest that iRobot Roomba Max 875 Combo With ThermaMist for $799: As Roomba’s new top-line robot vacuum and mop, this model features 35,000 Pa of suction, as well as hot steam to pretreat stuck-on stains. However, what really sold me was the “no pre-clean pickup” advertised on the box. I’ve got pet toys, my teen’s sports equipment and shoes all over the floor, cords, and loose rugs; other robot vacuums I’ve tried have struggled with my household. The Max 875, however, moved through my house with ease—in fact, I was quite impressed with how well it powered through even the toughest robovac challenges, like shoelaces and a maze of tucked-in chairs around a table. It did fine on pedestrian stains on my LVP floors, like spilled coffee, but even with the ThermaMist and repeated returns to the scene, the 875 Combo couldn’t fully clean an area with dried wet cat food. Setup was also pretty buggy—I followed the manual, but the vacuum took off before I could add it to the app and map my house, trying to clean a random area on 14 percent battery life. It would then return to the dock station, charge for five minutes, and repeat this process for well over an hour. When I did get it connected to the app, it said it needed an patch but was unable to download it. I eventually got it to work by factory-resetting the machine and starting all over, but this process took more patience than I’d expect at this price point. —Kat Merck.

Recent findings suggest that iRobot Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $599: Like its fancier sibling, the Max 875 above, the Plus 678 had a bit of a buggy setup process that required several attempts and a factory reset. The Plus 678 also has the Max 875’s AI-powered stain pretreatment (though without the ThermaMist steam) and 30,000 Pa of suction for Roomba’s upcoming “SealForce” technology, which lowers a skirt around carpets to suction deeper into the pile. I tested this with three different types of rugs—a regular-pile wool rug, a loose washable rug, and a low-pile faux fur rug. It did well on the first two, but failed on the third, becoming fully stuck. (Most vacuums can’t handle this rug, so I don’t exactly fault it for this.) Other than the setup mishaps—which included false “brush roller failure” messages and a mapping attempt that left it turning around in circles in the middle of an open room for 20 minutes—this is a serviceable mop-vac with a feature list that’s hard to fault at this price. —Kat Merck.

iRobot Roomba Plus 575 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $499: After hearing about the futuristic Roomba growing up, I was excited to see one in action. During setup, I found that the battery cover unscrewed, but assumed it was intentional since no screws were included. It soon fell off, so I taped it; days later, it came off during cleaning and got lost, leaving the battery and cords exposed to debris and the wet mop. Not great. From the start, it struggled to map my home. Cleaning requires app routines, which I didn’t love, as sometimes I just wanted to be able to click a single room and go without having to create another routine. The routines were often ignored or stopped midway. A mop pad fell off on every single run, forcing me to retrace the machine’s path to find it in my home. It also got caught on cords and repeatedly tried to climb my cat tree’s base, getting stuck perpetually spinning until I had to manually move it. Edge cleaning was nonexistent; there was so much cat hair and dust near where the floor met the wall. After a month, it threw up and scattered debris whenever it crossed the ¾-inch thresholds to the bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom, so afterward I had to vacuum the mess it created—defeating the purpose. —Molly Higgins.

Mova P10 Pro Ultra Gen2 for $360: This robot vacuum was solid, and especially did a good job with cleaning corners (it got a 2 out of 3 on the corner test, capturing both the stool and fridge Cheerios), but it did a poor job scrubbing away the cherry juice for my stain tests. One of the two stains was almost entirely left behind, and overall on casual runs of the vacuum it didn’t feel as if my floors were super clean. Still, if you’re looking for good corner cleaning, and carpets more than hard-floor deep cleaning, this is a solid robot vacuum for the price.

Roborock Saros 20 for $990: WIRED reviewer Adrienne So was mostly happy with this robot vacuum, as was I. She noticed the super-high suction (it hits 36,000 Pa) actually caused more debris to be left behind on her hard floors when it passed over thresholds; I didn't have this problem with the thresholds in my home, but instead I found debris on my hard floors immediately after having this vacuum clean them, with no threshold required. It also only got a one out of three in my Cheerio test, which isn't great for such an expensive vacuum.

Recent findings suggest that tapo RV50 Pro Omni for $400: After testing several robovacs that made me want to chuck them out the window, I had high hopes for Tapo’s fresh model that was released this summer. It promised over four hours of run time, dual-laser obstacle avoidance, DeepEdge mopping for corners and edges, and automatic floor detection to keep mops off carpets. But during more than two weeks of testing, it never mapped my home correctly or fully cleaned it. It couldn’t cross the ¾-inch raised thresholds into my kitchen or bathroom, and it mapped my bedroom but detected a phantom obstacle and cleaned only the 2-foot entryway. My kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom were never fully cleaned during testing. It’d be heading for the dock to wash mops or empty them and would forget to do the hall next or finish the living room and begin charging again. About half the time, the app asked me to map my home again, apparently forgetting the previous day’s map. During mapping, it sometimes started cleaning, got lost, and then unveiled it couldn’t find its dock, leaving me to locate and return it. When vacuuming, it sometimes left the mops at the station, returned for them, forgot, and began charging, thus ending its task. Not once did it successfully vacuum and mop my whole home. Online reviews are glowing, so perhaps I got a dud—but this experience was enough to make me want to clean by hand instead. —Molly Higgins.

I test all robot vacuums in my three-story townhouse, where they clean across luxury vinyl plank (LVP); tile; carpet; and a large, low-pile rug. I have a dining table and four barstools to navigate, and both a cat and a child who create daily messes. I run the vacuum at least three times across the main floors of my home to assess its overall performance and note any recurring challenges or errors it encounters. I do pick up my son’s toys, but I like to watch how the robot navigates the various chair legs and side tables throughout my home, and whether it sucks up the power cords beside my bed. I also like to see how much battery life is left after a run is complete on each level of my home.

My corner test, using three Cheerios in three corner (or cornerlike) spots.

I also set up an obstacle course of sorts. The first one is the corner test, created by three Cheerios placed in three tricky corners on the middle floor of my home: one in the corner of an Ikea Billy bookshelf toe kick, one underneath my countertops next to the fridge, and one next to a barstool chair leg. It’s how I test how well each robot vacuum gets into corners and underneath cabinetry.

My spill test, with two spots of cherry juice on the floor.

I also create intentional spills for these vacuums to clean up. I use maraschino cherry juice to create two spill spots, then use a paper towel to smear and thin the stain to better replicate a spill you might not have seen on your floors. Many robot vacuums have AI that promises to detect these kinds of stains, but so far, no vacuum has stopped and scrubbed both spots on its first try.

Can You Use Robot Vacuums on All Kinds of Floors?

Sources indicate that you can, especially since there are so many mopping models now to better clean hard flooring. You can use these devices on anything from hardwood to LVP and tile, though I wouldn't recommend leaving smaller rugs out for these autonomous gadgets to get stuck on. Large, set rugs are fine, but bathroom and kitchen mats or any thin, easily moved rugs should be cleared out of the way and put in the wash instead of vacuumed by your robot vac.

How Often Do You Need to Maintain Your Robot Vacuum?

In a recent development, taking good care of your robot vacuum will help it last. Here’s the debris-removal process you should follow for each robot vacuum style.

Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely upcoming vacuum.

Do I Still Need a Regular Vacuum if I Have a Robot Vacuum?

According to recent reports, I recommend keeping some kind of vacuum on hand, though that can vary based on your home. If you have stairs, you’ll definitely still want a hand vacuum or stick vacuum that can easily maneuver and clean your staircase, while pet owners might want a vacuum that can clean upholstery. I prefer my Dyson stick vacuums for a good carpet clean, but your mileage may vary depending on your preferences. Either way, I think everyone needs a companion vacuum of some kind with a robot vacuum.

Do You Need a Self-Emptying Dock?

In a recent development, you don’t need it, but a self-emptying dock makes using a robot vacuum much easier. You aren’t fumbling with debris every time it runs, and having a single bag to remove or a bin to empty is much easier than pulling debris out of the vacuum itself. I’d even recommend choosing a stick vac with a self-emptying dock, as it just makes the whole experience so much easier.

Industry observers note that how Does WIRED Obtain Robot Vacuums? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?

Recent findings suggest that almost all the robot vacuums we test are provided to us as press samples with the understanding that there is no guarantee of coverage or type of coverage. Most companies don’t want a used vacuum back, so we either donate them locally or have the top performers long-term tested to see how they last.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), remarked Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace.
  • His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), remarked Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.

His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.

The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys mentioned they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he notes.

Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you blueprint it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its looks last month.

“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.

According to recent reports, more than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was released in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne notes.

According to recent reports, the ICO stressed the importance of owners understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.

“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement.

#3141. Tech Report: Thuma Dupes: Japanese Joinery Bed Frames That Stack Up (2026)

📅 10 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2402 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Thuma Dupes: Japanese Joinery Bed Frames That Stack Up (2026)

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese joinery bed frames are bolt-free beds made from notched wood pieces that slide and click together to make a stable frame.
  • Recent findings suggest that thuma is the leading brand in this space, and we love its product lineup—several members of the WIRED Reviews team have tested Thuma beds, and all rave about them.
  • According to recent reports, japanese joinery is a traditional carpentry method that uses only wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard).

Japanese joinery bed frames are bolt-free beds made from notched wood pieces that slide and click together to make a stable frame. Think Jenga, but with really nice, sleek wooden furniture. The advantages are many, starting with easy assembly that takes just a few minutes and requires no tools.

Recent findings suggest that thuma is the leading brand in this space, and we love its product lineup—several members of the WIRED Reviews team have tested Thuma beds, and all rave about them. However, they’re not cheap. A Thuma bed frame starts at $895 for a twin frame with no headboard, and the king-sized Thuma signature bed our testers loved costs $2,500.

According to recent reports, japanese joinery is a traditional carpentry method that uses only wooden components. Instead of nailing boards together, each piece of wood is carved so it snugly fits into openings carved into neighboring pieces—the “joints,” if you will. The tension and strong hold of the interconnected pieces create structural integrity.

It’s a pretty easy way to channel your inner Bob the Builder, and the finished bed frame looks stunning in its simplicity. However, we are always on the lookout for products at the intersection of high quality and low price—curious to see if any contenders could give Thuma a run for its money—so we researched and tested, and these are our findings.

Recent findings suggest that be sure also to check out our guides on the best mattresses we’ve tested, as well as the best pillows and bedsheets. You’ll need something to put on your new frame, after all!

Updated November 2026: We’ve added two newly introduced bed frames to this guide and ensured accuracy throughout.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard).

I’m a longtime fan of DreamCloud mattresses, so it came as no surprise that the brand’s Japanese joinery bed frame is excellent. Like the mattress, this frame has numerous thoughtful details that stood out immediately.

DreamCloud made setup seamless. Each piece is labeled, and when it comes time to put it all together, take a gander at the endpoints of the long pieces. If you look closely at the joints where they intersect at the ends, you will see holes drilled into the top and bottom pieces. Small rods attach to the boards and fit into them, serving as a secondary mechanism to ensure stability. I find this impressive because the beams stack neatly into the grooves carved into the ends. In a word, it’s crisp. It’s a tiny detail, but the frame stayed virtually silent when I put a mattress on it or moved around in my sleep. I didn’t notice any shaking, either.

Sources indicate that another excellent feature is the frame’s center stability beam (crucial for preventing long-term sagging), which slides in last. This lets you avoid nesting it before closing the frame, unlike some other Japanese joinery models from different brands. It’s far more convenient.

Lining up the slats is the most challenging part of the process; you have to make sure everything is aligned perfectly. To help the process go smoothly, you’ll find wooden rods—similar to those on the ends of the boards—in the center of the bed, where you insert the slatted frames. They’re about the width of a pencil. Pop those slats in, unroll, Velcro to keep in place, and go.

You don’t need a headboard with this frame, but DreamCloud provided one for testing. Two square openings are located inside the top beam of the frame, right where your head would be. The headboard slides into these internal slots, which hold the end pieces and keep it upright. Foam block stickers are included to be attached last, so your wall doesn’t get scuffed up. All that, and still no tools necessary. Down to the details, people! And this detail you don’t want to skip—it’s around $449 for a queen. The headboard costs $299 extra, but even with that, it’s still far cheaper than luxury alternatives. You’ll also have two stain options: natural or a very pretty walnut.

That noted, you’ll have to consider how many sleepers will use this frame and the weight of the mattress you’ll place on it. When I was testing newly introduced mattresses every week, two of the frame’s center support legs split right down the middle. Make sure you don’t screw them on too tightly, as I suspect the tension is what made the wood look like I had been chopping it with a small axe. Regardless, I was shocked to see this happen, and it is another notch on Thuma’s belt for heightened durability. —Julia Forbes.

The Bamboo Bed Frame by DreamCloud ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard).

Recent findings suggest that silk & Snow is another brand that I hold in high regard. Every time I’ve tested a mattress from the brand, it consistently packs quality for the price. This platform bed frame was no exception. There are two options: natural rubberwood and acacia wood. I opted for the latter, which is a medium-brown color. I thought that the stain was stunning, with a richness akin to a lovely latte. However, I really appreciate that they offer options not just in wood stain color, but also in the actual hardwood itself.

Recent findings suggest that this frame arrived in four separate boxes. I liked this approach because it protected the wood stain’s integrity during shipping. Every other frame in this guide was packed into one box—not unlike a mattress-in-a-box, but heavier and longer. I actually preferred this route, as every box was also labeled for easy setup.

Recent findings suggest that like the DreamCloud frame, Silk & Snow’s doesn’t require tools or hardware to set up—it’s made entirely of wood. One thing I learned the hard way: Make sure the center beam is within the frame perimeter before fully closing it off. Then place the slats into the internal notches on the side rails, and it’s ready for a mattress. I had no problems with noise, shaking, or feeling unstable. It supported a mattress just fine, and I am still truly enamored with how the wood stain looked amidst my studio’s decor.

However, I do a lot of testing, so I’m constantly setting up and taking down mattresses, frames, and bedding. This is where having two people will be crucial, as I decided to do it all by myself for the sake of time, to the detriment of the frame. The frame got badly scratched up around the slatted portions where the corners of the boards stack together, due to my awkward solo assembly motions. I doubt you’ll be doing this as much as I do, but it was still a bit disappointing to see. Despite this, it’s worth recommending because I loved how it looked and performed. —Julia Forbes.

The Silk & Snow Wooden Platform bed frame ranges from $550 for a twin to $900 for a king (frame only).

According to recent reports, the Avocado City Bed Frame is a minimalist wood (blonde or walnut) platform frame with a completely tool-free Japanese-joinery assembly process. The same natural, nontoxic, and sustainable materials practices that guide the tech giant’s mattresses are at play here as well.

The City Bed is regularly $1,299 for a queen, and it is the most affordable of Avocado’s bed options (though you have to factor in a shipping fee). It’s made from very nice, solid wood (I tested the walnut version). There’s an optional headboard that I did not test. The bed itself is attractive, fairly subtle, and unobtrusive. In fact, if your duvet is reasonably large, you may not even see much of the bedframe.

The frame fits together using interlocking joints with metal reinforcements. In my testing, it’s been solid and sturdy, with no squeaking or any signs of weak joints. It is a tight fit at times, especially at the four corners, and I had to tap it with a soft mallet to get it fully flush (which sort of defeats the no-tool promise, but you probably could have done the same with a copy of Infinite Jest or something equally solid). —Scott Gilbertson.

The Avocado City bed frame ranges from $750 for a twin to $1,499 for a California king (frame only).

Industry observers note that the Birch frame was the most basic of the Thuma dupes I tested. I was really excited about this one because the wood is sourced from the land of the pines, otherwise known as my home state of North Carolina. Poplar is a durable hardwood, and southern yellow pine is one of the harder pine woods. (I can attest to this because, for an eighth-grade science project, I tested the durability of regional woods.) The manufacturing partner is a certified member of the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC). The legs are made of a completely different wood, Appalachian maple. It also uses a soy-based resin to remain completely formaldehyde-free.

It arrived in two boxes, and setup was quick and easy—the step-by-step instructions were the most thorough of the bunch. With written descriptions and pictures, it’s hard to mess this up. Plus, you don’t need any tools to get this frame up and running. The outer boards were polished to maintain the gorgeous hue of the pine wood. However, be cautious when handling the inner slatted-board sections, as this wood is not finished. I got a small splinter and was not a happy camper. Next, I set up the bed and slept on it for a week—the standard amount of time I test mattresses. The first few days, this thing creaked and moaned like crazy. It didn’t feel stable, and I was shaken if I moved even slightly. By the end of the week, it seemed to fall into place and settle, so I no longer noticed the noise or motion.

According to recent reports, I don’t want to discount this as a possible option, though, because the wood quality was what I wanted it to be, and so was the overall price. If you’re looking for a cheaper option for a guest room, upgrading your teen’s room, or furnishing a first apartment on a budget, this could work well for you. —Julia Forbes.

The Birch Madison bed frame ranges from $749 for a twin to $978 for a California king.

Nectar Sleep (queen, frame only).

Nectar Sleep (queen, with bamboo headboard).

I had never set up or slept on a Japanese joinery-style bed frame before testing this model from Nectar, and now I’m a true believer. The frame is made from bamboo, and assembly took just about 20 minutes with no tools required.

In a recent development, putting it together was super simple: the four feet had cut-out notches where the frame slid into place, and you just needed to push down to make the pieces lock together—it’s essentially like putting together a giant set of Lincoln Logs. After sliding the footboard into the feet’s notches, you finish both sides the same way by pushing down into the notches. The middle section is springy and has a floating foot to adjust for the bed’s pressure, so no cumbersome box spring is needed. The slats are connected with Velcro and just need to be unspooled and adhered to the sides. I opted for a headboard that slides in from above and stays in place because of the cutouts on the head portion of the frame below.

I’m physically disabled, so putting together furniture with tools and nails or screws is nearly impossible. I recommend that anyone who’s in a similar position check out a Japanese-style bed frame, as it’s lightweight, requires no additional tools, and requires very little physical strength. Plus, this frame comes in two colors, has optional headboard attachments, a 60-night home trial, a two-year warranty, and free shipping. —Molly Higgins.

The Nectar Bamboo bed frame ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Here’s the thing: Thuma is still a Japanese joinery bed frame. Therefore, I’d be remiss not to include it on this list. While I can vouch that the options above are credible dupes, many of my teammates feel nothing beats the original in this case.

Recent findings suggest that thuma’s Classic Bed Frame is made from upcycled, sturdy rubberwood that comes in four finishes: walnut, natural, espresso, and gray. You can also choose different headboard variations, including all-wood, a pillow board (Italian wool and foam), or a hybrid of the two. The design’s not only beautiful, but it’s also backed by certifications such as UL GreenGuard Gold and CertiPur-US (if you opt for the pillow board).

It has been revealed that WIRED Gear Editor Julian Chokkattu has had his Thuma frame for several years, and he notes it takes next to no time to set up. He also loves that it doesn’t creak or slide—just a strong sense of security while sleeping on it.

The Thuma Classic bed frame ranges from $895 for a twin to $1,495 for a California king (frame only).

Just like with the best mattresses we regularly test, each frame required a week of testing (not including naps) to evaluate night-over-night performance. This also allowed time for the frames to settle into place and perform alongside the bed each was paired with.

How Do I Set Up a Japanese Joinery Bed Frame?

It has been revealed that your bed frame should come with installation instructions, whether it features Japanese joinery construction or not. In the same vein, I recommend having someone assist you with the setup. As mentioned in our Silk & Snow review, this helps mitigate the risk of bumping and scratching your fresh furniture.

Are These Bed Frames Better Than Thuma’s?

We wouldn’t say better, just different. Each brand offers its own approach to creating a bed frame that adheres to the Japanese joinery method. This could include the type of wood used, the stains offered, the types of headboards you can pair it with, where it was manufactured, and, of course, the price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

It has been revealed that if you ask any Mac admin for a list of the software on their fleet, they’ll pull up their device management inventory and show you the apps they’ve deployed. Ask them what their developers installed with Homebrew last month, which VS Code extensions they are running, or what npm pulled into a project on Tuesday, and you’ll get a different response. That software was never procured by finance, never approved, and never inventoried. It’s also where a growing share of the risk lives in the AI era. Workbrew 2.0 treats that gap as a problem worth solving for IT teams.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Industry observers note that device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

That used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Recent findings suggest that workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The firm notes it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

The part that is critical for everyone who isn’t a developer is the upcoming Workbrew app, a native Mac app for finding, installing, and updating approved software. Workbrew calls it “the app store for your entire tech giant.” Employees can browse what IT has approved, install it without opening Terminal, and request anything that isn’t on the list. IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

The app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of customers’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every blueprint, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

Industry observers note that with Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

Chris Merrell, Director of IT, End User Services, Camping World.

In a recent development, workbrew isn’t a device management tool and isn’t trying to be one. Your device management system deploys the Workbrew agent, and Workbrew handles software your device management system lacks visibility into. If your fleet consists entirely of office workers on managed apps, there’s nothing here for you. If you have developers, or you’ve noticed the marketing team installing things to run AI scripts, you have the problem whether you’ve discovered it or not.

AI tools have changed how we think about app management, because apps get installed differently now. Workbrew 2.0 provides IT with a list of development tools on the Mac and gives employees a sanctioned way to get what they need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, picking a gaming mouse can be difficult. There are countless metrics to factor in and a nearly unlimited number of mice with unique approaches in defining what's best. Quite honestly, it’s a market rife with opportunities for analysis paralysis to take hold.

That’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t. I can’t say precisely which mouse will work for you—that’s dependent not only on technical specs but on your preferences, needs, budget, and hand size—but hopefully I can provide some insights into the top options out there, what's the best for specific types of gamers, and why I’ve picked them.

Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse, Best Gaming Headsets, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Hall Effect Keyboards.

Updated November 2026: I've added the Razer Basilisk V4 Pro and Wallhack M-001. I've also included the Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike in my honorable mentions, reorganized the list, and updated prices.

The Razer Cobra HyperSpeed (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is far more reasonable and practical than most of the ultra-light options today. Instead of shaving down features and mass to make the simplest mouse possible, the Cobra Hyperspeed finds an ideal middle ground, maintaining features like RGB lighting, Bluetooth connectivity, and options for wireless charging. Despite that, it still weighs below 70 grams, a number that was unbelievable for even the most premium wireless mice a decade ago. Inside, it’s packing an optical sensor, optical switches, and an optical scroll wheel—all top-of-the-line parts that are some of the fastest and most reliable on the market. While the mouse is limited to 1,000-Hz polling with the included low-profile USB-A dongle (which I prefer for convenience), it can be upgraded to 8,000 Hz with the bulkier and less-convenient HyperPolling dongle, cutting out its only serious limitation.

Beyond that, this mouse can do practically everything. It works as a travel mouse, a permanent desktop solution, and is even compatible with Razer’s wireless charging pucks, which lets you charge the mouse using either the Mouse Dock Pro, which ups your polling rate to 8,000 Hz, or the HyperFlux V2 wireless charging mousepad. The simple, symmetrical shape is comfortable and easy to hold, with the curved buttons on top creating spots to rest your fingers, while the low, gradual curve feels natural for resting your palm. Plus, its near-symmetry means it can be used as an ambidextrous mouse in a pinch (although lefties will miss out on the side buttons).

While the price may be steep, Wallhack’s M-001 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best I’ve tested in a long time. Although the specs aren’t quite cutting-edge (the sensor is a bit outdated, and some of the internals are still mechanical instead of optical), every aspect of this mouse’s user experience has been fine-tuned to perfection. That's what sets it apart for me.

Sources indicate that the mouse itself is made entirely from magnesium, and the outer shell doesn’t feature any of the large weight-saving cutouts used by similar mice from Corsair, AngryMiao, and even Razer. Instead, the upper is entirely solid, and all of the cutouts are on the underside of the mouse. Because of this, the battery can be swapped out within seconds.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the mouse itself, the M-001’s dongle is one of the best on the market. Instead of simply sitting on a desk, this dongle incorporates physical dials to adjust the mouse’s sensitivity and polling rate, and recharges the spare battery when not in use.

In a recent development, while it may be silly, my favorite feature of this mouse is the swappable batteries themselves. Similar to a Nintendo Switch cartridge or an SD card, the batteries feature a push-lock mechanism that’s robust, satisfying, and intuitive, improving significantly on the magnet or rotation-lock systems that other swappable mouse batteries use.

The Rival 3 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is a simple, no-frills gaming mouse. It’s lightweight, robust, and pretty much hits all the marks for gaming: Easy-access side buttons, clicky main buttons, underside RGB lighting, and a grippy rubberized scroll wheel. This SteelSeries mouse doesn’t innovate much, but like a Toyota Camry, it’s simple and reliable enough to get nearly anything done. At a price below $50, you’re getting all the performance you can realistically use for non-professional gaming. There aren’t any unnecessary features that add complication, and the mouse can be fully disassembled in under five minutes with a set of Phillips and Torx screwdrivers.

The Razer Viper V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the latest installment in a long line of fantastic competitive mice, offering performance improvements across every metric. Along with top-of-the-line specs, optical sensors across the board, and a great symmetrical shape, the V4 also incorporates the same spherical dongle included with the Deathadder V4 Pro, which maintains its 8,000-Hz polling while adding LED indicators for information like connection quality, battery life, and DPI stage.

Recent findings suggest that using the exact same shape as the V3, this mouse is comfortable and intuitive to use. The shape is easy to move around, with small curves on the mouse buttons for your fingertips to rest, and the curvature of the sides creates natural spots for your thumb and pinky. The Razer Synapse software is one of the most powerful and intuitive on the market. There are customization options for mouse dpi, tracking distance, dynamic sensitivity, and even adjusting the mouse sensor to accommodate a rotated grip.

Sources indicate that the only downside of the Viper V4 Pro is how uncompromising it is— there's no Bluetooth, and the included 2.4-GHz dongle requires a USB-A to USB-C cable (included) that runs to your computer, with no option for a smaller USB-A dongle (last seen on the V2). These decisions were made to lighten the mouse and improve connection quality, but they can be inconvenient if you need a wireless gaming mouse to pair with a laptop.

The Infinity .97 is one of the lightest mice I’ve tested at only 48.3 grams (without the removable rear panel, which adds 3.8 grams), and one of the sturdiest thanks to its magnesium upper shell. While the skeletal shape may look off-putting at first, it was far more comfortable and usable than I would have expected, especially when used with a fingertip grip. However, anyone dedicated to a palm or claw grip will likely be better served by a larger mouse with a sturdier back end.

Industry observers note that beyond weight, this mouse has fantastic specs: 8,000-Hz polling, optical switches, and a rating of 0.2 ms of latency all put it on par with Razer and Logitech’s best offerings. The most impressive feature by far is the removable and magnetically hot-swappable batteries that recharge using the mouse’s 2.4G dongle. This eliminates downtime from a dead battery and reduces the risks of long-term battery degradation and failure (assuming AngryMiao continues to sell spares).

Recent findings suggest that while the styling is certainly more of an acquired taste, the large gaps result in a shape that’s rigid and better-looking than the usual uniform, hexagon-shaped holes. The shape is shockingly comfortable despite the gaps (which are placed to preserve typical touch points), and the removable rear “hatchback” panel finds a reasonable balance between a standard shape and the ultra-lightweight “fingertip mice” that have become more popular in recent years.

It has been revealed that the software is also shockingly robust, with expected adjustments for DPI, polling, macros, and so on, alongside more granular adjustments like debounce speed, motion sync, ripple correction, and a Blast Mode that sets the mouse’s internal sensor to its maximum speed of 20,000 Hz. (It’s worth noting that the mouse still communicates with your computer at 8,000 Hz—this simply provides more data from the sensor to the mouse). Also, unlike some similarly-priced offerings, this mouse has both 2.4G and Bluetooth connectivity.

The Basilisk V3 Pro was a fantastic mouse, and the V4 Pro significantly improves the technical specs while maintaining some of the best features. Primarily, the V4 Pro has an absurdly-high 8,000-Hz polling rate and a scroll wheel with smooth, ratcheted, and “high-sensitivity” scrolling options. This mouse also maintains the same four-button layout on the side, and has a larger shape with an integrated thumb rest for comfortable long-term use.

Sources indicate that as far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question. The mouse wheel also has horizontal scrolling that’s activated by tilting it to the left or right, and the large number of programmable side buttons are great for both gaming and multimedia editing. While it’s still fairly hefty at 98 grams, this mouse is great if you’re either ambivalent about weight and want something more ergonomic, or if you prefer a heavier mouse. It might not be worth an upgrade when coming from the previous model, though, given the price.

The Pro X Superlight 2C is only marginally smaller than the standard Superlight 2, and weighs 51 grams, a 15 percent drop. It's essentially a scaled-down version. They are both capable of 8,000-Hz polling, use the same 44,000 dots-per-inch Hero 2 sensor, and have the same quoted 95-hour battery life. Because the 2C packs all this into a smaller package, it’s ideal for people with smaller hands, or anyone who primarily plays using a claw grip and doesn’t need the extra weight.

It's not a travel-size mouse, but I think the 2C is better suited than most ultralight mice on this list. It uses a small USB-A dongle that can slot into a removable panel on the underside of the mouse for transport, and the shell is fairly sturdy. I wouldn’t toss it into a checked bag at the airport or wedge it into a side pocket, but it should hold up for light travel.

A larger, sculpted alternative to the Viper V4 Pro, the DeathAdder V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a fantastic mouse that’s a tiny bit heavier, but potentially more comfortable than its smaller cousin. If you prefer the shape and feel of a sculpted mouse, this is a great alternative to Razer’s flagship competitive model that packs comparable performance and is equally-loaded with premium optical internals. The two share the same in-depth customization options, with adjustments for sensitivity curves, lift-off and landing distance, and the ability to adjust the mouse’s rotation for different grip styles.

In a recent development, the Deathadder V4 Pro also introduced Razer’s spherical USB-C dongle with three RGB lights that can be adjusted to display information like polling rate, battery level, connection quality, or DPI. While the colored light system can be a bit abstract, it provides functionality to an accessory that’s going to be on your desk no matter what, and makes it easier to keep track of the settings on this ultra-lightweight mouse. Plus, I find it looks a lot more natural than most dongles available today. Much like other competitive-focused options on this list, the only real glitch with this mouse is the lack of Bluetooth connectivity, a weight-savings measure that makes sense for competitive use, but can be a bit annoying for certain users and setups that demand more flexibility.

Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike for $200: This is a major advancement in mouse tech, so much so that I’d consider it one of the most significant gaming mouse developments in recent years. This technology replaces the typical mechanical or optical switches under a mouse’s main buttons with analog switches, similar to those on a Hall effect keyboard, that allow for the actuation distance of the button to be customized. Because these linear switches no longer have a “click” sensation, the Superstrike pairs them with artificial haptic feedback. This activates when the button registers an input, and the intensity of the feedback can be customized across X levels.

However, I don’t personally like this mouse. The haptic feedback feels uncanny, since it shakes the entire mouse instead of creating a real “click” sensation, and the added complexity isn’t worth the relatively minor fine-tuning capabilities. However, I can recognize the benefits of the technology, and I can absolutely understand why some people might love this mouse.

Steelseries Rival Pro Wireless for $180: While the specs aren’t groundbreaking compared to other light mice, and the “ultra-polling” technology doesn’t offer a proven benefit over competitors, the Rival Wireless maintains the fantastic shape of previous installments in the Rival 300 line. If you’ve found other sculpted ultralight offerings from Razer and Logitech to be a bit lacking, this could be the option for you.

Sources indicate that razer Basilisk V3 Pro for $120: Razer’s previous installment in the Basilisk line is still a really solid option. This mouse is comfortable, convenient, loaded with features, and it looks sleek on any desk. It’s also featured in our Best Ergonomic Mouse guide, but it performs so well that I had to include it here. Razer’s optical sensor is capable of up to 35,000 dpi, and the mouse has polling up to 1,000 Hz (or up to 8,000 Hz with a HyperPolling dongle). As far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question.

Corsair Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight for $200: When I first reviewed the new 36-gram Sabre, I was wowed by its weight but critical of its overly thin shell and flimsy construction. However, I accepted these as being a part of its innate nature as the lightest-possible mouse, and I’m incredibly glad that it exists. It’s a great option if you’re willing to sacrifice everything in the name of “simplifying and adding lightness,” as car designer Colin Chapman put it. But it's probably not the right choice if you want something that feels substantial or meaningful beyond that.

Corsair Sabre V2 Carbon Fiber and Magnesium for $170: While neither of these carry the same groundbreaking lightness of their predecessor (they both hover just below the 60-gram mark), they offer a much more refined design with premium materials and rigidity that’s unmatched by Corsair’s mainstream competitors. While they lag a bit behind in performance, they both feel fantastic to fling around a desk while providing a much more sturdy chassis that gives the impression they can withstand some serious use. Unless you really love the looks or science of carbon fiber, the less-expensive magnesium chassis is definitely the way to go in terms of both sturdiness and on-desk appeal.

Logitech Pro X Superlight 2 Dex for $150: This sculpted mouse predates the Deathadder V4 Pro by over a year and, because of this, the specs lag slightly behind it. However, the shape is just as comfortable, and the internals are still fantastic for anyone except the absolute most-discerning. The best part of this mouse is that, these days, it can easily be found on a significant discount. If you don’t want to shell out the extra cash for Razer’s latest model, or if you prefer Logitech’s software and styling, this is the mouse for you.

Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for $70: While MMO-focused mice aren’t finding themselves in the spotlight anymore (much like many of the MMOs that required numpads, and even numpads themselves, for that matter), there are still a few new models kicking around. The Scimitar is one of the most modern ones, adding adjustability to the classic numpad-on-the-side formula with a sliding rail to accommodate different grip styles and hand sizes. While this mouse obviously doesn’t compete with other models on this list in terms of technical specs or weight, it’s a really great mouse for the kinds of games that still necessitate having swathes of macros at your fingertips.

Steelseries Aerox 3 for $100: While it doesn’t have nearly the same weight or speed advantages as offerings from Razer and Logitech, the Aerox 3 is still a great mouse in its own special way. Weighing in at only 66 grams and being one of the only waterproof mice on this list (I literally ran it under a sink for a couple minutes to test this), this mouse is great for multi-user gaming computers, accident-prone individuals, and/or the poolside gaming setup of your dreams. Plus, built-in Bluetooth connectivity means you aren’t stuck with a dongle! However, 1000 Hz polling and 18,000 DPI do mean that, if you aren’t looking for something that’s more durable than average, you may be able to get a good bit more performance for a comparable price.

It has been revealed that logitech G203 for $20: Budget gaming mice often forgo a lot of the conveniences and performance you get out of nicer models, but the Logitech G203 never feels like it's lacking. The sensor has a lower maximum sensitivity than you'll get out of a more expensive offering—8,000 dots per inch—so if you need that top-end sensitivity, you'll want to look elsewhere, but it features six buttons, compatibility with Logitech’s G Hub software, and, most importantly, has RGB lighting. Those are all things you'd typically expect to pay more for.

According to recent reports, razer Viper V3 Pro for $100: The previous-gen Viper V3 Pro remains a good choice for competitive gamers, especially since it's selling for much less than the newer model. It remains an uncompromising mouse for lightweight, high-speed gaming performance. Despite being a couple of years old at this point, it still has competitive specs, the same great symmetrical shape, and some of the best-feeling buttons on the market. The battery lasts an incredibly long time (it’s rated for over 95 hours, and I didn’t need to charge it once during my testing). And with the included HyperPolling dongle, the mouse is capable of up to 8,000-Hz polling.

One of the cheapest things you can do to upgrade your PC gaming experience is to invest in a high-quality mousepad. If you’re a mouse-and-keyboard gamer, having the right surface for your trusty little rodent can be super helpful. Not only do you have a nice little area of your desk cordoned off for mouse use, but you also get a surface designed to be as friction-free and slick as possible—so you’ll be as quick as possible.

The pebbled leather is supple and has a nice texture, but your mouse will glide over it effortlessly. It comes in three sizes and three colors.

SteelSeries QcK Mouse Pad for $11: SteelSeries’ QcK mousepad is one of my all-time favorites. The medium size is perfect for most desks, even small ones. It’s well-made and doesn’t fray easily—cheaper mousepads often fray at the edges, which ruins the aesthetic a good mousepad can lend to a workstation.

Industry observers note that grovemade Wool Felt Desk Pad for $70: This doesn't seem like your usual gaming accessory, because it's not. It's a wool felt pad from Portland, Oregon, organization Grovemade, and it's large enough to fit a keyboard and a mouse with room to spare. It feels soft and plush under your wrists, and all of the gaming mice on this list just glide over its surface; it's like they're sliding on glass. It's a big surprise, honestly. It's an easy and affordable way to inject some unique style into your work (and play) space.

What Makes a Good Gaming Mouse?

Here are a few features that really separate a gaming mouse from a regular came-with-my-PC kind of mouse:.

Extra-sensitive optical sensors: Gaming mice should have more sensitive optical sensors that can detect smaller movements more quickly than a standard mouse.

Sources indicate that more buttons: At a minimum, a good gaming mouse should have a clickable scroll wheel, a button for adjusting sensitivity, and two buttons where your thumb rests. Those extra thumb buttons can be lifesavers in competitive games.

Recent findings suggest that better buttons: They should also have higher-quality buttons, and more of them, than a standard office mouse. The left and right buttons should have individual switches inside, tensioned to register rapid clicks and reinforced to withstand more frequent clicks than a normal mouse. Top-of-the-line gaming mice often feature proprietary mechanical switches inside that give them a more tactile feel when you click.

Polling rate: For most games, the typical 1,000-Hz polling rate will be sufficient, but if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games, where split-second actions can be crucial to victory, than you may get some benefit out of mice with faster polling rates.

It has been revealed that don't buy the DPI hype: Dots per inch (DPI) is a metric that describes a mouse’s overall sensitivity. A higher dpi means it can respond quicker, which is helpful in competitive online games. However, even if your mouse can go all the way up to, say, 20,000 dpi, most people (even in online games) keep their sensitivity around 1,000 to 1,600 dpi. More doesn’t necessarily mean better.

Your Palm Size and Grip Style Matters.

A major aspect when shopping for a gaming mouse is size. Using a mouse that’s too small for your hand can cause strain on your hand and wrist, while a mouse that’s too large can feel unwieldy and be difficult to move precisely. It’s crucial to measure your hand and take into account the grip style you proposal to use.

There are three primary mouse grips: Palm grip, claw grip, and fingertip grip. Palm grip is typically considered the most accurate but least agile, and it’s how most people use their mouse day-to-day. Your entire hand sits on the mouse, with your palm resting on the back half and your fingers laid along the mouse buttons. Claw grip is more agile, but will sacrifice some accuracy and stability. For this grip, you rest the bottom of your hand against the mouse while bending your fingers into a claw-like shape, leaving a significant amount of open air between your fingertips and the back of your hand. Fingertip grip has the least contact and allows for the most agility, but also sacrifices even more stability. With this grip, your hand will hover over the mouse, with your fingertips resting on the mouse buttons, and your thumb and pinky finger gripping the mouse from either side.

Recent findings suggest that for a standard mouse used with a palm grip, the best way to determine the correct size is to measure the distance from the tip of your middle finger to the bottom of your palm, and compare those numbers to an online guide. Rocket Jump Ninja has a helpful tool for this, which also provides measurements of the recommended mice for cross-referencing. Alternatively, I’ve found it helpful to hold your hand in an arc as if you’re holding a mouse, and measure the distance from the bottom of your palm to your fingertips to get a measurement you can directly compare to mouse length. This method can also work for claw grip, but since the bottom of your palm will be resting directly on the mouse instead of sitting at the back, I find it better to err on the side of caution and pick a mouse that’s a few millimeters longer than you need.

Industry observers note that mouse sizing is dependent on the type of mouse you’re looking for: Whether chasing lightness or portability, there are quite a few short and small mice on the market. Compact or fingertip-grip mice like the Razer Basilisk Mobile or the G-Wolves Fenrir won’t fit the standard recommendations of mouse measurements. Instead, for a mouse like this (or any mouse you plan to use with a fingertip grip), I find it best to compare the mouse’s width to the distance between your thumb and your pinky finger (or your ring finger, depending on how you hold a mouse) in a comfortable gripping position. A mouse that’s too narrow can cause strain on your hand, while one that’s too wide can be difficult to properly grip and move.
