Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S.
  • Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.
  • Sources indicate that aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure.

Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.

Sources indicate that aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30.

Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace.

Employees are expected to move into the megafactory in January, and production is slated to begin by the end of 2028, according to AFP.

Satellite connectivity has become increasingly important to everyday life as well as national security.

It provides internet access to remote locations and defense equipment like warships and fighter jets, and lets governments and militaries communicate securely where Earth-based networks are unavailable or disrupted.

According to recent reports, the importance of such capabilities has become particularly apparent in Ukraine, as the country's military relies heavily on Starlink connectivity to fight Russian forces. Recent restrictions to the service over Russian-occupied territory reported by Ukrainian officials further underscored the way geopolitical conflict may depend on commercial businesses.

But Europe still has a long way to go in challenging Starlink's dominance.

SpaceX notes it has more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, making it by far the largest satellite constellation in the world, and aims up to 100,000 satellites.

Among the challengers is Amazon, whose satellite business, Amazon Leo, has deployed over 400 satellites and aims an initial in-orbit constellation of more than 3,200.

In a recent development, meanwhile, French Eutelsat operates more than 600 satellites in low Earth orbit through its OneWeb constellation. The organization is also part of the SpaceRISE consortium alongside SES and Hispasat, tasked with developing and operating IRIS².

The European Commission has called IRIS² a "strategic asset to achieve space sovereignty in the face of commercial satellite constellations, such as Starlink." The aim is for first launches to take place by the end of 2029, with initial services expected soon after.

In August, the Commission and SpaceRISE consortium unveiled they were expanding the main constellation from 282 to 348 satellites, increasing its secure communications capacity for EU governments by 60%.

Defense and security applications were the main drivers of the expanded scope, the Commission stated.

#3091. Breaking: Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients

Breaking: Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (454 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the company’s LINK device.
  • In a recent development, elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the firm announced.
  • "We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink unveiled on X.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the company’s LINK device.

In a recent development, elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the firm announced. The study represents a more advanced step in the company's efforts to develop a brain implant that allows people with paralysis to control devices using their brain alone. It will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement.

"We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink unveiled on X. "This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.".

Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the organization revealed that its first participant with ALS named Bradford Smith was able to communicate using brain signals alone. "Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people," Smith noted at the time.

Recent findings suggest that we've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.

Those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more:https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR pic.twitter.com/Vor7iXXCBA.

— Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026.

The FDA authorization was granted on an experimental basis, but it's a key step forward for Neuralink's LINK brain-implant system. The study will evaluate the ability of patients to control digital devices through thought, "with a focus on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life," Neuralink wrote. It will also assess the system's long-term safety and reliability.

WIth Neuralink's latest system, the tech giant's N1 implant is surgically placed in the skull, then the company uses its R1 robot to insert flexible electrodes into the brain. Neural activity from the brain associated with movement is then interpreted by software, which translates signals into commands for controlling computers or digital devices. The technology is designed to help patients communicate with the outside world, with the eventual goal to let them operate devices without keyboards or other physical controls.

In a recent development, neuralink said patients with ALS may be eligible for the LINK trial, but it didn't specify other requirements or the number of participants. It now has approval recruit participants, then conduct the study under an approved clinical protocol. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

#3090. Tech Report: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

Tech Report: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working.
  • According to recent reports, as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices.
  • In a recent development, as an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

According to recent reports, as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:.

In a recent development, as an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

Sources indicate that accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

According to recent reports, aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

It has been revealed that last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

In a recent development, greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”.

My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

In a recent development, below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

In a recent development, I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

According to recent reports, I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

According to recent reports, above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

Industry observers note that since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

Industry observers note that I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

According to recent reports, when I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

When I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is right now a Logitech MX Master 3S.

To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought fresh in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a big purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

In a recent development, tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

Sources indicate that I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

Industry observers note that the bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

In a recent development, this is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

Sources indicate that the paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

The rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it said that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!).

Sources indicate that welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

In a recent development, my office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

Sources indicate that an iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

In a recent development, absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now rolled out, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

According to recent reports, this image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo (previously Moonlight and Sunshine).

According to recent reports, you may also notice that my desk, from a company called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

At night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me manufacturer). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

So sure, I do work here sometimes.

Industry observers note that my wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both major gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

Industry observers note that the desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just remarked “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

Sources indicate that the main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

As for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

Then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

In a recent development, I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

#3088. Samsung’s R95H TV indicates what RGB LED is capable of

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1474 w)
📖 Baca

Samsung’s R95H TV indicates what RGB LED is capable of

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The excellent matte screen and ability to display a vast amount of colors makes the R95H one of the top RGB LED TVs available.﻿.
  • Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
  • If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The excellent matte screen and ability to display a vast amount of colors makes the R95H one of the top RGB LED TVs available.﻿.

Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Industry observers note that RGB LED TVs finally became affordable in 2026, and there’s always a lot of promise when latest TV technologies come out. More color, higher brightness, improved performance — RGB LED TVs have a lot to prove. The Samsung R95H does a lot to deliver some of those promises. It can display more colors than other TVs I’ve seen so far this year, and the combination of light output and its matte screen makes it great for a bright room. RGB LED TVs might still be in their infancy, but the R95H is a solid TV that demonstrates off the benefits of the new backlight tech.

Industry observers note that because RGB LED TVs use individual red, green, and blue LEDs for their backlight (instead of a field of white or blue LEDs), they can deliver more colors than LED TVs. The Samsung R95H is one of the best examples of this in RGB LED TVs. It can fully display all the colors used in the vast majority of movies (which use the P3 color space) as well as the few that use the wider BT.2020 color space.

Matte screen handles reflections incredibly wellGood color accuracy in Filmmaker mode.

Some color crosstalk in white textGrayscale leans a bit cyanNo Dolby Vision support.

The accuracy of those colors is also really good in HDR (it’s not quite as good in SDR, because the TV overbrightens most of them). Some earlier reviews called out mediocre color accuracy on the R95H, which I experienced with the first sample Samsung provided me in June. Samsung replaced that sample because I was worried something was wrong with it. But in Filmmaker mode with firmware version 1247 on my current 65-inch TV, I was pleasantly surprised by the R95H.

HDR formats: HDR10 Plus, HDR10, HLG.

HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), up to 8 with Wireless One Connect box (sold separately).

Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Digital, Auracast, Q-Symphony.

Gaming features: VRR (up to 165Hz), ALLM, Game Bar, FreeSync Premium Pro.

Sizes available (inches): 65, 75, 85.

Sources indicate that colors are wonderfully lifelike. The green of the jungles in Planet Earth II, which uses the expanded BT.2020 color gamut, is beautifully vibrant, as are the hummingbirds that populate the trees. With movies that use P3, the foliage in the demo material on the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc doesn’t have quite the same brilliance, but it still looks accurate and lifelike. Skin tones are natural. White and gray tones, like those in snow scenes, have a slight blue tint. It’s pretty minor, though.

The R95H also has a good amount of light output — a full-field white screen measured 694 nits, while specular highlights hit 2,206 nits in Filmmaker mode (the TV’s most accurate picture mode). That’s similar to the Sony Bravia 7 II but short of the Bravia 9 II by a few hundred nits, and well short of the TCL X11L. Flagship 2026 OLEDs also have brighter highlights but dimmer full white screens, as is expected from OLED panels. Black levels on the R95H are really good for an LED display. There’s a bit of blooming, but not as excessive as I’ve seen on some RGB LED TVs this year. Overall, the Samsung R95H delivers an impactful image.

The matte glare-free finish on the screen limits reflections well. I was never distracted by seeing the ceiling lights reflecting, as I can be with glossy screens. The black-level raise problem — where ambient light gets caught behind the matte coating, causing the screen to look more gray than black — is much better. With a bright room, the black level rises a small amount, but it’s not washed out, and dark images still have depth.

Industry observers note that I had a great time gaming on it, too. Some earlier reviews noted challenges with smearing, but recent firmware seems to have addressed this for the most part. While racing in F1 24 in 120Hz mode, motion was smooth. The TV struggled a bit more when I set the Xbox to 60Hz, but I still enjoyed playing.

One inherent issue with RGB LED TVs, though, is color crosstalk — I’ve seen it to some extent on every RGB LED TV, though it’s least apparent on the Sony Bravia 9 II. It can happen when there’s a dominant color onscreen near a lighter color, such as white text, lighter skin tones, or white clouds. The dominant color can bleed into those lighter colors, influencing their tint. This happens a bit on the Samsung R95H. It’s most noticeable with white text. I saw it with news tickers on a red background, making the text look subtly pink, and with gaming, particularly while playing No Man’s Sky. Text displayed above a large yellow hologram has a slight yellow coloration that disappears if I move my view away from the hologram. In fleeting moments, it’s not too distracting, but when the color around the text is consistent, the effect is noticeable.

Some TVs avoid this by defaulting the backlight to white and relying on the color filter, as LED TVs have for years. While doing that gets rid of any possibility of color crosstalk, it also diminishes the TV’s color brightness and wider gamut. So with RGB LED TV technology where it currently is in its development cycle, there’s going to be a tradeoff between some color crosstalk or a more limited color gamut.

Industry observers note that the R95H still has the same limitations as all Samsung TVs. There’s no Dolby Vision support (Samsung is an original backer of HDR10 Plus and will likely never support competitor Dolby Vision). It also runs on Tizen OS, which is continually one of my least favorite interfaces. Everything is buried a click or two deeper than it should be, including input selection, which makes it cumbersome to use. The remote, rechargeable via both USB-C and the solar panels on the back, is small, and I’m not a fan of the button layout — they’re bunched together, and the volume control feels clunky to me.

Sources indicate that the R95H is also still more expensive than most of its competitors. The Sony Bravia 9 II has better processing and is brighter, although it also has more blooming than the R95H. If you can fit a 75-inch in your space, the TCL X11L is significantly cheaper since it introduced. I think it’s a better overall TV. Then there are the flagship OLEDs — Samsung’s S95H and the LG G6 — which are both less than or the same price as the R95H, depending on size. And OLED is still a step ahead of RGB LED in overall picture quality because of its better contrast.

There’s still room for RGB LED TVs to improve. With its wide color gamut coverage, good out-of-the-box accuracy, and excellent matte screen, the Samsung R95H is one of the better ones to come out this year. Put up against those RGB competitors, it makes a strong case. But OLEDs are still better overall performers with superior contrast, and even cheaper non-RGB LEDs can get you most of the way there for less.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge.

Industry observers note that I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.

For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

  • Those extra tools let adults in charge of teens see how much time their kids have spent on X and set a daily limit, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts the teen already follows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Any responsible adult should probably check on their teen's X usage.

Elon Musk's X has finally introduced parental controls for kids aged 13 to 17, allowing parents and guardians to manage their teen's experience on the platform. Teens' accounts will now default to protected mode, with sensitive media restricted and targeted advertising blocked. The upcoming settings will also give families "additional tools on top of those defaults," the platform announced.

Those extra tools let adults in charge of teens see how much time their kids have spent on X and set a daily limit, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts the teen already follows. They can also filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, allow parents to control who can send direct messages, and see which accounts their teen has chatted with one-on-one (without seeing the messages themselves).

Recent findings suggest that to use the newly introduced parental controls, follow the guide in X's help center. "Linking starts with the parent or guardian and finishes with the teen. Both consumers have to agree," the platform states.

In a recent development, X emphasized that the new controls let parents manage content without prying into their kids' lives. "Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account," the company wrote. Parents will be able to control up to five teens' accounts.

There are reasons that parents should probably keep teens far away from X. In the last five years, it's been rife with problems including hate speech, AI-generated CSAM, misinformation, deepfake images, a lack of moderation, unauthorized AI training, propaganda, algorithms that amplify partisan content, AI bots, human trolls, and the omnipresence of awesome role model Elon Musk.

Even X admits that it's not aimed at kids or teens. "While X is not designed for or promoted to children, and users must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here," the organization wrote. While claiming that "child safety is a top priority at X," the platform likely introduced the upcoming rules to comply with current or future regulations in multiple states and countries.

SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.
  • In a recent development, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center.
  • According to recent reports, but can space-based data centers for AI really work?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.

In a recent development, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center. SpaceX filed its application at the beginning of the year, presenting the initiative called Starmind as the better alternative for ground-based data centers. In its filing, the firm argued that "orbital data centers are the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power," since they use "solar power with little operating and maintenance costs.".

According to recent reports, but can space-based data centers for AI really work? Critics doubt they can. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and a critic of Elon Musk's space and AI ambitions, told AP that "it's not going to happen. The idea behind sending AI data centers outside our planet is so that they don't consume resources their ground-based counterparts do, like energy and water for cooling.

Recent findings suggest that however, critics of the plan argue that space is a vacuum that traps heat inside objects and doesn't make cooling down hardware easier. In space, heat has to leave the satellites via radiation, and Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to radiating the heat out for all of them. In addition, that many satellites could cause in-orbit collisions and generate a huge amount of space junk.

According to recent reports, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr believes that with this approval, though, America is "leading the world into the era of super intelligence." It opens a "bold fresh frontier," he added. Under the terms the FCC has approved, SpaceX has permission to deploy satellites into orbital layers spanning 50 kilometers, at altitudes between 500 meters and 1,002 kilometers.

It has been revealed that the tech giant is required to deploy at lease one authorized satellite and place it into its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033. By the same date in 2035, it must have already deployed 100,000 satellites to their respective orbits. Three years later, on November 25, 2028, it must have already deployed 500,000 of the authorized satellites. All 1 million satellites must have already been placed in their assigned orbits no later than November 25, 2040. Musk previously said that SpaceX will start launching the satellites in 2027, but we'll have to wait and see if the company can stick to that timeline.

#3084. Tech Report: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1162 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.
  • But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.
  • "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.

But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.

"We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added.

In a recent development, ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he stated.

The investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.

Industry observers note that chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply.

But demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.

In a recent development, chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.

Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he remarked.

The scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.

The investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA.

"Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

"But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added.

Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.

Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets.

Sources indicate that "I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.

Sources indicate that that gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin.

It has been revealed that argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina.

In a recent development, brazil's case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix. About 89% of the country's electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025, according to the country's Ministry of Mines and Energy.

"That puts Brazil in a strong position to benefit as AI and data centers drive up demand," Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist and portfolio manager at Hightower Advisors, told CNBC.

It has been revealed that but while Brazil has the world's second-largest reported rare-earth reserves, its estimated mine production is far smaller than China's. USGS estimates put Brazil's output at 2,000 metric tons in 2025, compared with China's 270,000 metric tons. Brazil's reserves are estimated at 11 million metric tons by the USGS, second only to China's 44 million metric tons.

For investors, the gap between Brazil's vast reserves and limited current production is both the opportunity and the execution risk.

For investors, the policy question is whether governments can make projects viable and keep them on track.

Sources indicate that luis Costa, Citi's global head of emerging markets strategy, said governments need to offer incentives, particularly in the early stages of projects, because infrastructure lags the region's resource wealth. He also stressed that support must last: infrastructure projects can take several years to develop.

The World Bank's Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Update for 2026 projects growth for the region of 2.2%, and highlights the "restricted fiscal space, sticky inflation and high borrowing costs.".

"The economic policy and fiscal policy needs to get in line as markets are globally becoming more sensitive to fiscal stories," said Costa.

According to recent reports, brazil will need to establish fiscal credibility to attract investment, particularly if higher public spending puts additional pressure on debt and borrowing costs. "If investors doubt the government can stabilize public debt, companies' long-term financing costs could stay high even as the central bank lowers its policy rate," Ch added.

With Argentina set for national elections in October 2027, political continuity will also matter for energy investment. "A return to tighter currency controls or persistent deficits would make companies more likely to delay projects, even in an oil field with attractive economics," noted Ch.

Pro-business President Javier Milei faces a tight race for re-election, though a change in leadership would not necessarily undermine medium- to long-term investment.

"There is also the possibility of a pragmatic Peronist ticket emerging, which markets would be satisfied with," mentioned Nicolas Jaquier, emerging-market fixed-income portfolio manager at Ninety One.

For those governing across Latin America, policies to unlock its wealth of resources will be key for it to emerge as a winner from the AI demand boom.

"Supply chain security is becoming more and more relevant, and if commodities take off Latin America can be a clear and obvious winner," said Kumar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.

It has been revealed that two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on. It’s as gorgeous as the pictures make it look, and the texture on the back of my “Capulet Olive” green colorway is the stuff of dreams. But the thing that sealed the new ultra-high-quality design for me wasn’t the comfortable curved edges or the textile back: it was the haptic motors.

In a recent development, now, don’t get me wrong. The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year. I’ll need to use it for just a bit longer to be 100% sure, but the pebble-like aesthetic of the curved front, back, and edges feels tangibly amazing to hold and use. It reminds me a bit of the Galaxy S3’s design, just without the nasty, slimy plastic back. It’s curved just enough to feel amazing, but not enough to be an annoyance like some waterfall display phones were in the past.

But a haptic motor is completely intangible to you as the reader. You can’t see it in pictures, and even if I describe it, you may not fully understand why it makes such a difference. If you’ve been using Google Pixel phones for a long time, you’ve probably forgotten how good a quality haptic motor can feel, but let me remind you for a moment just how key such an invisible thing can be to completing the experience.

It has been revealed that typing on the Signature 27 is pure bliss because of it. Tapping each key feels more like the press of a physical keyboard key. Unlocking the phone emits a satisfying light punch to my thumb, signalling a successful read. When I send a reply on X (Twitter), the button tap and subsequent animation feel like the message is being sent through the phone onto the web. It’s wonderful, and it’s one of the reasons people love the Pixel experience so much.

Unfortunately, the Motorola Signature 27’s haptic responses aren’t applied to as many parts of the UI as Pixel phones do, and that’s where the real miss comes in. Adjusting the brightness or volume doesn’t feel like a physically rotating vertical dial the way it does on Pixel, and I’d love to see Motorola add this in an patch. But at least the upgraded haptic engine is a huge step in the right direction for Motorola and a good way to make the Signature 27 feel like a proper flagship phone.

Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems.
  • It has been revealed that A newly introduced study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material.
  • Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to latest sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

It has been revealed that A newly introduced study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.

In a recent development, the researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

Recent findings suggest that the simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.).

Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

It has been revealed that regionally, over half of the total CO2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

Sources indicate that if peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 (About DOIs).

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
  • It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.

It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

Industry observers note that chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.

It has been revealed that the interim final rule was confirmed by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.

Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.

Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that the change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people stated it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the fresh BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes.".

"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he remarked.

U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.

Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

The app’s latest upgrade will turn half the display into a keyboard for tiny typing.

In a recent development, edovia's Screens is a remote desktop app, which gives you a way to control your computer for the iPhone, iPad, another Mac or even the Vision Pro. Screens 5.10.6, its latest patch, adds the ability to turn your iPhone Duo into a tiny MacBook when it's in a partially open, clamshell configuration. #3076. Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.
  • Industry observers note that there are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth.
  • In a recent development, “There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.

Industry observers note that there are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth. But another major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched when it comes to re-creating the feeling of a bustling, real-world city, and GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is the studio’s most lifelike setting yet. It has functioning buses and trains, plentiful buildings you can go into and explore, residents you can chat with, and huge areas where you can interact with wildlife far away from the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City. For Emma Fraser, an assistant professor at UC Berkeley who studies urban ruins and virtual cities, the sense of realism has created a unique sensation while playing.

In a recent development, “There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she says. “Because you have these moments where you think, ‘I’m in a place, I’m experiencing a location.’ You comprehend intellectually that it’s not real or that it’s at best a representation, but you still have this feeling in your brain and you’ll still dream about being in that place.”.

It has been revealed that fraser teaches courses on topics including urban geography and virtual worlds and has written papers exploring topics like “mapping in the digital age” and “the virtual spectacle of the end of the city.” She claims she started researching video game cities in part because, despite their influence and reach, they’re an underexplored space in academia. “I’m a geographer, and geographers are obsessed with cities,” she explains. “So much of geography is thinking about: How do we imagine cities? How do we navigate cities? How do we build cities? How do we map cities? And video games have all of that, but they’re not taken that seriously as an academic interest.”.

Recent findings suggest that like much of the world, she’s been looking forward to GTA VI for years, particularly because of Rockstar’s on-the-ground approach to research. Before development on the game began, developers from the studio traveled to Florida to get an accurate picture. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me, the starting point for the game was the setting, rather than the story or characters. “We just went around to feel it out,” he stated. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate.”.

While there are plenty of open-world games, many of the most successful — from Elden Ring to The Witcher — are sent in fantastical spaces. GTA stands apart in how its various settings look and feel true to the real world. And Fraser believes that this is one of the key reasons the series has such universal appeal. “You know immediately how to function in a city,” she explains. “You know there’s going to be law enforcement, there are going to be city blocks, there are going to be pedestrians, cars, and buses. It’s this really interesting environment that gives you a lot of possibilities to get a player more immersed in your world, because they already know a lot about a city as a general concept.”.

“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time.”.

Fraser describes GTA VI’s world as having “implied expansiveness.” It’s not a one-to-one re-creation of the real location. There are plenty of things missing; you don’t see schools or daycares, and parking spaces are relatively sparse. But the game gets enough details right to be recognizable. Fraser explains that as long as certain parts of the city look correct — the lighting, the coastline, the decoration of street corners, the major arterial roads — that’s enough to convince people that they’re in something resembling Miami.

Recent findings suggest that “You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time,” she says. “Instead it’s these highlights. What [Rockstar] do very successfully in the game is those snapshots. They’ve got far more content that is recognizable as Florida or Miami than they’ve been able to fit into previous games. So it’s a much more overwhelming sense of being in that place.” The “implied expansiveness” also comes in the form of dialogue, radio programs, and TV shows that suggest a much bigger world by discussing places and moments that exist outside of the game you can actually explore.

In a recent development, this level of verisimilitude — combined with the fact that players can explore the city from multiple perspectives, everything from walking to flying a plane — has led to an experience that Fraser likens to virtual tourism, which can result in all kinds of different playstyles. “Some tourists are going to blow a lot of money on taxis and get to wherever they’re going as fast as they can,” she explains, “and some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place.” Similarly, there are certain players who will just experience the story and play through the main missions, and others who will get lost in side activities like bird watching.

“Some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place”.

What’s also notable about GTA VI is how its relationship-focused premise is motivating some players to experience the world in a much less violent way. And that includes how they move through the city. Some people are driving more carefully to avoid killing civilians, while others are exploring spaces while both characters hang out together. “In the first few games, you’re this empty vessel. You’re a criminal, you’re doing criminal things,” claims Fraser. “Whereas with GTA VI your motivation and the way you think about your character is really important.”.

Now that the game is out and millions of players are venturing through Vice City, Fraser is hoping to use it to research the ways that real and virtual worlds intersect when it comes to how we navigate cities. GTA VI offers a lot of choice in this regard; you can still steal a Lambo and speed through the streets, but you can also hop on a train, put on some headphones, and listen to a podcast while getting where you need to be. “Because this world is so fully furnished, and you have so many options, you might start to import your own real-world practices into the game,” she says.

It has been revealed that but at this point, what has struck her most is the attention to detail that separates the universe of GTA VI from its contemporaries. “You can’t just generate a generic city and stick icons in, which is what a lot of games do,” she explains. “You aren’t going to get a sense of a real place if you do it that way.”.

Motorola has posted an updated list of devices getting its Android 17 upgrade, with a few updates already available and many more left to go.

With the revision now rolling out to select devices, most recently the Razr Fold, Motorola is confirming an official list of devices getting Android 17.

The list was posted by Motorola Brazil, so this includes devices Motorola doesn’t sell in US markets, and also lists Razr devices without their year naming scheme, rather their international branding – i.e. “Razr (2026)” is “Razr 70.”.

As per usual, Motorola’s update rollouts may see timing vary by region. The Razr Fold update, for example, is currently rolling out in some international markets but has yet to land in the US.

Here’s the full list of Motorola devices officially confirmed to be getting Android 17:.

Motorola explains what’s newly introduced in Android 17 as follows:.

Among the latest features of Android 17 are improvements to the system interface, with more customization options, new icons, and changes to the layout of buttons and widgets. The Settings menu has been redesigned to make navigation more intuitive and facilitate access to the smartphone’s main functions.

Artificial intelligence in everyday life.

With the upgrade, Circle to Search now offers real-time translations, allowing you to understand content in other languages ​​more easily, without having to interrupt your current activity on your smartphone.

Simplified connectivity and sharing.

Android 17 enhances connectivity with Instant Hotspot , which simplifies sharing your internet connection between compatible devices. Quick Share has also received improvements to facilitate file transfer, including compatibility with iOS smartphones via QR Code.

Industry observers note that security remains a top priority for the system. The Authentication Failure Lock , a security feature in case of theft, locks the screen after unsuccessful authentication attempts. Meanwhile, Message-Based Fraud Detection enhances the identification of potential threats and fraud. Furthermore, access to emergency calls has become easier and faster.

More control over the visual experience.

The revision also improves HDR brightness control, which adjusts the screen intensity to highlight bright details in compatible photos and videos. Users can adjust this brightness for more comfortable viewing, or even disable the feature.

The Motorola Signature 27, the firm’s latest flagship, ships with Android 17 out of the box.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An alleged latest video reveals Galaxy S27 dummy units that look like the latest leaks, and Samsung fans aren’t having it.

At this point, it’s anyone’s best guess as to what the Galaxy S27 series looks like, but it’s seeming surer and surer that Samsung will be giving the series a major redesign this coming year. Chris Franklin, a writer at SammyGuru, posted an unboxing video of the Galaxy S27 on X, citing that there’s a possibility the unboxing is AI-created — there are some eyebrow-raising reflections here, but it’s hard to tell for certain. The design looks similar to the “confirmed” renders that leaked a few days ago, although there are some subtle differences.

According to recent reports, I don't think much about the design of phones, they're essentially all the same, especially when considering you're looking at the front 90% of the time, but I've always found the Galaxy's vertical camera layout to be the least attractive of any of the major phones. I think this looks much better.

Unsurprisingly, another leak from earlier in the month has a similar look but, again, with subtle differences. So far, all the major leaks in the past few months are pointing to Samsung outfitting the Galaxy S27 series with a raised camera island that looks extremely similar to Apple’s design on the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro series.

Industry observers note that samsung isn’t alone here. The Xiaomi 18 series and Honor Magic 9 Pro series both have eerily similar designs, and many other 2026 and 2027 phones have followed suit. The most obvious problem with Samsung’s potential design (and, by extension, Apple’s) is the raised camera lenses, which protrude above the raised camera island. Xiaomi’s island is flat, following Google’s idea that a camera bar should protect the lenses and also keep the phone from wobbling or feeling off-balance.

Drama has already taken off on X (formerly Twitter), where Noah Cat reposted the video, and it seems Samsung fans aren’t happy. Samsung has needed to change up the vertical camera bar for years, as it has regularly gotten in the way of Qi2 and MagSafe magnetic accessories. This newly introduced design might help that, but it seems fans wanted Samsung to return to the Galaxy S10 horizontal camera bar days, not this new iPhone-esque raised island.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype demonstrates off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the newly introduced HiLight LED in one.
  • I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED.
  • Recent findings suggest that images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype demonstrates off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the newly introduced HiLight LED in one.

I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED. I didn't use the temp sensor much but it was handy if whenever I was sick and wanted to check my temp without jamming an under tongue temp stick or wasting money on a temporal temp device -- because my phone already had one in it!

Recent findings suggest that images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The device is seen with the markings that are common to other known Pixel prototypes, with the key difference compared to the final model being the fact that the camera bar has both a temperature sensor and HiLight.

We can tell this is HiLight due to the diffused rear LED, and we know this isn’t a Pixel 10 Pro XL because the camera bar has full-width glass instead of a metal portion.

Google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. While the sensor was never particularly beloved, Google did see backlash from the lack of functionality in HiLight at launch. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.
